headline: Efficient and resilient systems for machine learning, from wearable devices to warehouse-scale computers
intro: Running a machine learning model costs energy, hardware, and time. These costs decide where a model can run and who can afford it. PEARL studies the runtime systems, memory hierarchies, schedulers, and compilers that set them. We build systems that run demanding models on the hardware people already have. Our work spans wearable devices, edge servers, and warehouse-scale computers.
closing: Efficiency decides who can use machine learning. When a model runs cheaply, it can serve a clinic, a classroom, a field station, or a phone.

thrusts.title: Efficient serving of large generative models
thrusts.stake: A model is trained once, but it is served for as long as it stays deployed.
thrusts.blurb: Every request to a large language model (LLM) consumes GPU memory, compute, and energy. Serving systems often leave a processor idle, keep redundant tokens, and apply one numerical precision to the whole model. Each of these choices wastes hardware or work. We restructure the serving stack in four ways. First, we overlap CPU and GPU execution. Second, we reorganize and reuse the key-value cache. Third, we drop tokens that leave the output unchanged. Fourth, we choose numerical precision for each layer and each timestep.
highlights: APEX: asynchronous CPU–GPU execution for online LLM inference on memory-constrained GPUs
dLLM-Serve: memory management for serving diffusion language models
HiRED: attention-guided token dropping for high-resolution vision–language models
DiffPro: joint timestep and layer-wise precision optimization for diffusion inference
HydraCache: LLM inference prefill parallelization through distributed cache blending

thrusts.title: Inference at the edge
thrusts.stake: Many applications must run inference near their data, within tight deadlines, over unreliable links.
thrusts.blurb: Clinical monitoring, industrial inspection, and radio access networks often need answers within milliseconds. Their data must sometimes stay on the device for legal or safety reasons. Sending every request to a data center breaks these deadlines and constraints. Running the full model on the device exceeds its memory and energy budgets. We partition models across the device, the edge server, and the cloud. We decide what to quantize, what to execute speculatively, and what to transmit. Our systems keep latency-critical computation next to the sensor. They call on remote resources only when the accuracy gain justifies the cost.
highlights: SWEET: workload-balanced edge inference through quantization and partitioning (NSF, with Queen's University Belfast and University College Dublin)
SLED and WISP: speculative decoding and batching that meets service-level objectives in distributed edge serving
Polymorph: energy-constrained multi-label classification of video streams on embedded devices
MARVEL: automated generation of custom RISC-V extensions for a given model class
Transformer inference acceleration on RISC-V for edge deployment
Network slicing: scaling and placement of edge servers in open radio access networks (O-RAN)

thrusts.title: Memory systems and accelerator utilization
thrusts.stake: Accelerators are scarce and expensive, yet they often sit partly idle.
thrusts.blurb: Cloud providers often give each tenant a whole accelerator, and many tenants use only part of it. When a job's working set exceeds fast memory, the slowest memory tier sets its speed. Both problems stem from scheduling and memory-management policy. We build mechanisms that share accelerators safely among concurrent workloads. We predict page accesses before demand faults occur. We also place data across memory tiers automatically, without programmer effort.
highlights: ParvaGPU: spatial GPU sharing for large-scale deep neural network inference in the cloud
Stride-aware page prefetching for GPU unified memory through Markov pattern prediction
Memory tiering in the Python virtual machine
Application-attuned memory management for containerized high-performance computing (HPC) workflows

thrusts.title: Agentic methods for high-performance code optimization
thrusts.stake: Scientific codes often reach a fraction of their hardware's peak performance, and few experts can close the gap.
thrusts.blurb: Domain scientists write most scientific software, and performance engineers are scarce. Large language models can propose code changes, but the proposals may run slower or compute wrong results. We build multi-agent systems that analyze code, propose transformations, and measure each one. A change survives only when measurement validates it. Benchmarks and correctness guarantees are part of the research itself. Undergraduate researchers contribute substantially to this work.
highlights: MARCO: multi-agent code optimization for HPC
FACT: compositional CUDA kernel synthesis grounded in CUTLASS C++
LLM-guided runtime parameter optimization for energy-efficient inference
AI-driven autonomous experimentation for turbulent flows
Parallel Islands: an educational instrument for parallel computing

thrusts.title: Resilience and energy accounting at scale
thrusts.stake: At scale, hardware faults are routine, and energy is a first-order design constraint.
thrusts.blurb: A silent wrong answer does more harm than a visible crash. Large parallel jobs typically recover from a fault by restarting from a global checkpoint. Energy is usually measured for the whole machine. Global restart wastes the work of healthy processes. Machine-level energy readings hide which stage or input drives the cost. We measure energy per execution stage, input modality, and instruction. We build recovery mechanisms that let a long-running computation survive component failure without restarting from the beginning. Our goal is to make the cost and correctness of a computation predictable before it consumes substantial machine time.
highlights: Modality inflation: energy characterization of multimodal LLM inference
Power Log'n'Roll: power-efficient localized rollback for Message Passing Interface (MPI) applications
SAFIRE: compiler-driven parallel fault injection (with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory)
Dynamic precision iterative refinement
